definition.question: What is the evangelical debate over mental health?
definition.html:
Evangelicals broadly agree that people with depression, anxiety and other mental illnesses deserve the church's care. They disagree over what mental illness is and who should treat it. The biblical counseling movement holds that Scripture is a "sufficient rule for the presuppositions, principles, and practices of counseling" and denies "that the findings of secular psychology make any essential contribution" to it, in the words of the Association of Certified Biblical Counselors covenant. Christian integration, represented by the American Association of Christian Counselors, joins "biblical truth, clinical excellence, and compassionate care" and treats people as "physical, social, psychological, and spiritual beings." A third emphasis, closest to medicine, stresses that mental illness is illness and that therapy and medication should carry no stigma.

In church life the question usually comes down to referral, medication and what a congregation offers. See what pastors and churchgoers report and short answers to common questions.

faq.label: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.title: Mental Health and the Church, Briefly Answered

items.q: Is mental illness a spiritual problem, a medical problem, or both?
items.a: Many evangelical writers answer some version of both, but they weigh the parts differently. Ed Welch of CCEF, writing for Ligonier, lists five possible causes of depression (our own hearts, other people, our bodies, Satan, and God's sovereign purposes) and advises helpers to treat depression first as suffering and "remain agnostic about its causes." Biblical counselors stress the spiritual roots; integrationists and Christian clinicians give more weight to the body and the brain. The answer shapes whether a church mainly offers prayer and counsel or also urges professional treatment.

items.q: Is it wrong for a Christian to take antidepressants?
items.a: Writers on both sides of the counseling debate allow it, with different cautions. Desiring God's piece by physician Kathryn Butler (2019) says God "has gifted us with medical science as a means of common kindness" and that, "when carefully combined with counseling and spiritual disciplines, antidepressants can ease some of us back into daylight," though "we should never rely on medication exclusively." Welch writes that people "are free to take medication" but warns that it "cannot address spiritual matters." In Lifeway Research's 2017 survey, 26% of churchgoers said their church encourages medication for mental illness and 6% said it discourages it; most said their church has no opinion or were not sure. See the chart.

items.q: Can prayer and Bible study alone overcome serious mental illness?
items.a: Many Christians have believed so. In a 2013 Lifeway Research survey, 35% of Americans, and 48% of evangelical, fundamentalist or born-again Christians, agreed that with "just Bible study and prayer, ALONE," people with serious mental illness like depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia could overcome it. Ed Stetzer, then Lifeway Research's president, answered that Christians "forget that the key part of mental illness is the word 'illness.'" No position on this page discourages prayer; they differ on what else belongs beside it.

items.q: How often do pastors talk about mental illness?
items.a: More than they used to. In Lifeway Research's 2021 survey of Protestant pastors, 43% said they speak about acute or chronic mental illness in sermons or large group messages several times a year or more, up from 33% in 2014 (when the question asked only about acute mental illness). The share who rarely or never do fell from 49% to 37%. The same survey found 26% of pastors say they have personally struggled with some type of mental illness. See the chart.

items.q: What can a church do for people with mental illness and their families?
items.a: Nearly all pastors think it should do something: 89% in Lifeway Research's 2021 survey said local churches have a responsibility to provide resources and support for individuals with mental illness and their families. The most common step is a list of experts to refer people to (68% of pastors say their church keeps one), followed by a plan for supporting families (40%). Fewer offer training for leaders to identify symptoms (20%) or have a counselor on staff skilled in mental illness (18%). Churchgoers often see less of this than pastors describe; see the comparison.

items.q: Do churches know when someone is at risk of suicide?
items.a: Often they do not. In Lifeway Research's 2017 study, about a third of churchgoers (32%) said a close acquaintance or family member had died by suicide, and only 4% of those said church leaders were aware of their loved one's struggles. Yet 86% said their church would be a safe, confidential place to disclose a suicide attempt or suicidal thoughts, and 80% of pastors said their church is equipped to assist someone who is threatening suicide.

items.q: What does the Bible say about depression and despair?
items.a: Scripture gives voice to anguish without treating it as unbelief. Psalm 88 ends in darkness; Psalm 42 asks, "Why are you cast down, O my soul?"; Elijah asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4); Job cursed the day of his birth (Job 3); and Jesus said in Gethsemane, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38). Writers in all three positions on this page draw on these texts to say that lament is a form of faith, not its absence.
